https://www.padilla.senate.gov/newsroom/: WASHINGTON, D.C. — U.S. Senators Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), Ranking Member of the Senate Committee on Rules and Administration, Mark R. Warner (D-Va.), Vice Chair of the Select Committee on Intelligence, Susan Collins (R-Maine), Chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, and Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.), Chair of the Committee on Rules and Administration, introduced the bipartisan Election Infrastructure Security Act (EISA) to provide states and localities with a more reliable source of funding to secure American elections. The legislation would repurpose the largely unused Presidential Election Campaign Fund (PECF) to support critical election security needs, including cybersecurity improvements, voting equipment upgrades, and protections for voter registration systems. State and local election officials often lack the consistent federal resources needed to maintain secure and reliable election systems. Currently, federal election security funding is limited and unpredictable, forcing election officials to rely on already-strained state and local budgets to address evolving threats, replace aging equipment, and maintain critical infrastructure. This legislation would allow election officials to make long-term security improvements, proactively address vulnerabilities, and avoid costly emergency upgrades. “American elections are safe and secure, but in a time of rising threats at home and abroad we will ensure they stay that way with the right investments in our election infrastructure,” said Senator Padilla. “Our bill would rededicate an existing, but widely unused, voluntary fund to ensure that localities have the resources to support election needs – like improved cybersecurity and voting equipment upgrades. As Ranking Member of the Senate Rules Committee and California’s former Secretary of State, I recognize that robust and reliable federal funding for elections is a top priority, and I’m proud to support this is commonsense, bipartisan legislation that will help further build up the strength of our democracy.” “Free and fair elections are the foundation of our democracy. As Vice Chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, I’ve seen firsthand the threats facing our election systems and the critical role that state and local officials play in defending against them,” said Senator Warner . “Keeping our elections secure requires more than sporadic funding; it requires sustained investment. This bipartisan legislation would put an outdated, largely unused federal program to work strengthening election security by providing election officials with reliable funding to modernize voting infrastructure, address evolving threats, and ensure every eligible American can cast their ballot with confidence.” “Protecting the integrity of our elections is essential to maintaining public confidence in our democratic process,” said Senator Collins. “This bipartisan legislation would support that goal by providing a reliable source of funding to strengthen election security, modernize outdated equipment, and help ensure that our elections remain safe and secure.” “Election security is a fundamental responsibility of government, and states and local election officials need the resources to carry it out,” said Senator McConnell. “This bipartisan legislation would put an outdated federal fund to better use by providing a dedicated source of funding to strengthen election infrastructure, improve cybersecurity, and modernize voting equipment. It is a practical approach that supports state and local election administration without creating a new federal spending program.” The PECF was established to provide public financing to eligible presidential candidates through voluntary taxpayer contributions made on federal income tax returns. However, participation has declined significantly as candidates have increasingly relied on private fundraising. No major-party presidential candidate has used the program since 2008, leaving the fund largely obsolete. The Election Infrastructure Security Act would permanently convert the PECF into a dedicated Election Security Fund, providing states with a more predictable source of support to protect and modernize their election systems. Specifically, the Election Infrastructure Security Act would: Establish a dedicated Election Security Fund by converting the existing PECF into a program supporting state and local election security. States would receive a guaranteed minimum of $3 million annually, while territories would receive at least $600,000. At least 67 percent of the fund would be directed to local election jurisdictions, except in states that centrally administer federal elections; Support critical election security improvements by allowing funds to be used for broad purposes, including modernizing election technology, strengthening cybersecurity, upgrading voting equipment, protecting election infrastructure, reimbursing prior security investments, improving election administration, and shortening wait times. Funds cannot be used for litigation; Require transparent spending plans and accountability by directing states to develop plans outlining how funds would be used, tracked, and monitored, subject to a public notice and comment process; Modernize the voluntary taxpayer contribution system by increasing the federal income tax checkoff with adjustments for inflation from $3 to $5 for individuals and from $6 to $10 for married couples filing jointly; Place administration of the fund under the Election Assistance Commission (EAC), which already oversees federal election assistance grants under the Help America Vote Act ; and Strengthen oversight by requiring annual state reports on expenditures, equipment purchases, and program outcomes, as well as periodic EAC audits to ensure funds are used appropriately. The bill is endorsed by the Bipartisan Policy Center, Responsive Gov Action, Project for Election Infrastructure, and 23 state and local election associations, including the Arizona Recorder Association, California Association of Clerks and Election Officials, Colorado County Clerks Association, Connecticut Town Clerks Association, Florida Supervisors of Elections, Georgia Association of Voter Registration and Election Officials, Kentucky County Clerks Association, Louisiana Registrar of Voters Association Inc., Maine Town & City Clerks Association, and more. “The Election Infrastructure Security Act is a critical first step in ensuring that state and local officials across the country have the funding and resources they need to keep our elections secure and accurate. It turns a defunct box on a form into an opportunity for Americans to direct sustainable support to the dedicated people who keep elections running. This bipartisan legislation helps fund our elections like the essential infrastructure they are, and I commend the leaders of this bill for putting forward this innovative solution,” said Sam Oliker-Friedland, Chief Executive Officer of Responsive Gov Action. “Secure elections require modern infrastructure. This legislation provides a fiscally responsible way to ensure election officials have the tools, technology, and cybersecurity protections necessary to administrations elections safely and efficiently. Thank you, Senators, for your steadfast work in a solution that does not increase the deficit or impose new federal mandates, but ensures our elections are safe and secure,” said Sarah Hague, Executive Director of the Project for Election Infrastructure. “Bipartisan action to better fund elections is one of the most meaningful steps federal lawmakers can take to protect the security, accessibility, and accuracy of our elections. We’re asking election officials to run elections in increasingly complex threat environments, with fewer resources than ever before. Defending against these evolving threats requires continuous vigilance and sustained investment. This legislation would provide the stable, long-term funding election officials need to continuously strengthen the security and resilience of our elections,” said Kathy Boockvar, former Pennsylvania Secretary of State. “Confidence that election results reflect the will of the voters is the thread that holds our democracy together. This initiative would improve elections across America with no additional net federal spending, helping the tens of thousands of dedicated workers who run our elections to update outdated voting equipment, invest in cyber and physical security, and improve the accuracy of voter rolls,” said Former U.S. Senator and Missouri Secretary of State Roy Blunt. “The threats facing our elections are increasingly complex and constantly evolving – and election officials are on the front lines of confronting those challenges. They need reliable funding to stay ahead of the latest threats, strengthen election infrastructure, and communicate effectively with voters. The Election Infrastructure Security Act is a timely and, importantly, bipartisan investment in our election infrastructure. This is a consequential way we can support the dedicated public servants in Virginia and across the country who work year-round to administer secure, transparent, and accessible elections,” said Chris Piper, former Virginia Chief Election Official and Commissioner of the Virginia Department of Elections. As Ranking Member of the Senate Rules Committee with oversight over federal elections and California’s former Secretary of State, Padilla has been a vocal leader in protecting our elections. In September, Padilla released a statement after the Department of Homeland Security’s Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) released its 2026 Election Infrastructure Security Plan, ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. Padilla and Congressman Joe Morelle (D-N.Y.-25), Ranking Member of the House Administration Committee, also demanded the Trump Administration immediately restore funding to the Election Infrastructure Information Sharing and Analysis Center (EI-ISAC), which helps state and local election officials protect federal elections from cybersecurity threats and election mis- and disinformation campaigns. In June, Padilla and Senator Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) announced the State and Local Election Security Act of 2026 , legislation to provide up to $10 billion for state and local election administration to support election security and improve efficiency. WATCH : Padilla: “Her legacy will live on in every person who answers her call, ‘Si, se puede!’” WASHINGTON, D.C. — U.S. Senator Alex Padilla (D-Calif.) took to the Senate floor to honor the life of labor, civil rights, and feminist leader Dolores Huerta. Padilla celebrated Huerta’s legacy and underscored the lasting impact of her lifelong fight for workers’ rights and the empowerment of countless communities nationwide. “She was an icon and a true trailblazer, a pioneering labor leader, feminist, and advocate who dedicated her life to making the world a better place: fighting for workers’ rights, for voting rights, for health justice, for health care access, for environmental protections, and justice just fundamentally,” said Senator Padilla . “But what made Dolores extraordinary wasn’t just the causes that she championed or the victories that she helped secure. It was the countless barriers that she broke down and the doors she flung open for all those who would follow.” As a proud son of immigrants, Padilla highlighted Huerta’s impact on his own life and reflected on her labor advocacy helping working families, like his own parents, build better lives with fair wages. “As many of you know, I’m the proud son of immigrants from Mexico. My father is a proud UNITE HERE Local 11 retiree,” continued Senator Padilla . “So I grew up experiencing firsthand the impact of the fights that Dolores Huerta and generations of labor leaders have advocated for. Those fights helped make it possible for my parents to raise three children in a working-class community.” Padilla emphasized Huerta’s efforts to ensure future leaders, especially women of color, have opportunities to continue breaking barriers in leadership and advocacy. He recognized her lifelong commitment to advocacy, noting that she inspired future generations by protesting and organizing up until the end of her life. Padilla underscored the importance of carrying on Huerta’s legacy by continuing to fight for justice, organize, and live by her call, “Si, se puede!” “The truest measure of Dolores Huerta’s legacy isn’t found in the awards that she’s received. It’s found in the people that she inspired, the communities that she empowered, and the generations of leaders that she helped bring forward,” concluded Senator Padilla . “And the greatest tribute that we can pay to Dolores is to carry her work forward for future generations, to keep organizing, to keep fighting, to keep helping those who are facing injustice, to find their voice, and to keep opening the doors for those who come after us.” Full video of Padilla’s remarks is available here . Full transcript available below: Mr. President, the poet Bessie Anderson Stanley once wrote, “To know even one life has breathed easier because you have lived. This is to have succeeded.” And by that measure, Dolores Huerta’s life was an extraordinary success. Few people have made more lives breathe easier or opened more doors to a better, brighter future for more people than Dolores Huerta, whom we sadly lost last month at the age of 96. She was an icon and a true trailblazer, a pioneering labor leader, feminist, and advocate who dedicated her life to making the world a better place. fighting for workers’ rights, for voting rights, for health justice, for health care access, for environmental protections and justice just fundamentally. Dolores once said, quote, “We must use our lives to make the world a better place. That is what we were put on this earth for.” And I believe that’s exactly how Dolores used her life. But what made Dolores extraordinary wasn’t just the causes that she championed or the victories that she helped secure. It was the countless barriers that she broke down and the doors she flung open for all those who would follow. Dolores came of age at a time when women, especially Mexican-American women, were rarely expected to lead political movements or to negotiate with powerful business leaders or to challenge elected officials, both sides of the aisle, I might add. but inspired by her mother who was a business owner who exemplified women’s power by her example and she encouraged Dolores to get involved in her community. Dolores didn’t wait for permission to start making a difference. She simply rolled up her sleeves and got to work. As many of you know, I’m the proud son of immigrants from Mexico. My father is a proud UNITE HERE Local 11 retiree. So I grew up experiencing firsthand the impact of the fights that Dolores Huerta and generations of labor leaders have advocated for. Those fights helped make it possible for my parents to raise three children in a working-class community. There’s a reason why my siblings and I could see a doctor when we were sick, why my parents could afford to buy a home, and my dad could take time off of work each year for vacation. All because of a good union contract. Things that might seem ordinary to most, but for working-class families like mine, they represent the difference that a union makes. The difference that fair wages can make, and the difference that the ability to bargain collectively can make, and they’re part of the very future that Dolores spent her life fighting to build. She understood that the fight for a more just society went beyond the workplace. That fair wages means being able to put food on the table for your family and to keep a roof over their head. That worker protections mean being able to care for a loved one without losing a paycheck and being able to work and live free of harassment and discrimination. Dolores also understood that building a movement meant ensuring everyone had the opportunity to lead, especially those who has, who have historically been shut out of positions of power. It’s why she traveled across the country encouraging women, especially Latinas and other women of color, to run for office. She would recruit candidates, help them secure endorsements. She would knock on doors and campaigned alongside them, helping pave the way for new generations of women in public life. And no matter how many wins she achieved, Dolores never treated her work as finished. At the age of 89, she was arrested protesting for a raise for home care workers. And Dolores was still showing up at rallies, still walking precincts, and still talking with young organizers and encouraging people to vote well into her 90s. And I know she would have been so proud to see so many Americans turning out to exercise their fundamental right to vote in this year’s midterm election. Dolores continued doing all of this for as long as she was able to because she understood that building a movement isn’t something that you do once. It’s something that you have to keep doing over and over again, generation after generation. Time and again, Mr. President, Dolores Huerta has been recognized for her contributions to shaping a better, fairer, and more just nation. And as a result, her portrait hangs in U.S. embassies around the world. Schools in several states have been named in her honor. President Obama awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom to her in the year 2012. But the truest measure of Dolores Huerta’s legacy isn’t found in the awards that she’s received. It’s found in the people that she inspired, the communities that she empowered, and the generations of leaders that she helped bring forward. And the greatest tribute that we can pay to Dolores, is to carry her work forward for future generations. To keep organizing, to keep fighting, to keep helping those who are facing injustice, to find their voice, and to keep opening the doors for those who come after us. Yeah, Dolores may have been ahead of her time, but more importantly, she helped change the times. And her legacy will live on in every person who answers her call, “Si, se puede.” And her legacy will live on and on and on. Thank you, Mr. President. I yield the floor. ###

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senators Alex Padilla and Adam Schiff(both D-Calif.), both members of the Senate Judiciary Committee, released the following statement reacting to the introduction of the Judicial Understaffing Delays Getting Emergencies Solved (JUDGES) Act: “We appreciate the efforts by Senators Coons and Young to create new judicial seats that are sorely needed, and we have supported previous versions of this bill. However, the latest version of the bill now includes a poison pill provision to lay the groundwork for a split of the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals — long the dream of arch conservatives — which is unacceptable to us. “The Ninth Circuit operates efficiently, and this court’s opinions are deeply respected and crucial on issues related to immigration, the environment, technology, civil liberties and much more. But for years, the circuit has been targeted by conservative legal activists trying to weaken its influence and attack its reasoning. This provision seeks to help legitimize those harmful efforts under the pretext of judicial efficiency. “We appreciate the willingness of Senator Coons and Senator Young to work with us on this issue and look forward to continued conversations moving forward, but we want to be clear that we cannot support this bill while it includes this troubling provision.” ###

WASHINGTON, D.C. — Today, U.S. Senator Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), a member of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources and Environment and Public Works Committees, issued the following statement after voting against the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 : “I have long supported commonsense permitting reform and this bill includes many provisions that I support and even authored, particularly to streamline the permitting of transmission infrastructure. Unfortunately, it also contains provisions that would irreparably harm California and the 109 federally recognized Tribes who call California home. “The bill threatens Tribal sovereignty, and I am deeply concerned that it could allow the destruction of ancestral lands, sacred places, and cultural resources without adequate legal recourse for the communities that have relied on them for generations. It also asks us to rely on assurances from President Trump, who just weeks ago said he would not approve any wind projects – and lacks the enforceable safeguards to ensure renewable energy projects will be judged and approved fairly by the Trump Administration and that oil and gas drilling will not resume off the coast of California. “While the bill facilitates significant improvements to our electrical grid and I’m proud to have contributed to the language of the bill that will bring more energy supply online to meet growing demand, I cannot sacrifice the rights of Tribal governments or California’s environment. Though I must oppose this bill in its current form, I will continue the work to responsibly cut red tape on renewable energy, transmission, and critical infrastructure projects.” Senators Padilla and John Hickenlooper (D-Colo.) led Energy and Natural Resources Committee Democrats in drafting the transmission and grid reform section of the bill. This section will give the federal government the authority to approve more transmission lines faster, including by allowing transmission applications to be processed simultaneously with state reviews, so projects clear permitting sooner. Padilla co-led an amendment with Senator Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) to strike the changes in this bill to the National Historic Preservation Act, based on significant concerns from Tribal governments. California has the largest number of Tribes in the lower 48 states, with 109 distinct federally recognized Tribal governments. Padilla also submitted five amendments in an effort to improve the legislation, including: Amendment 6942: Ensures Tribes continue to have meaningful access to the courts through the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA). Amendment 6943: Ensures federal immigration detention facilities cannot proceed without judicial review. Amendment 6936 and 6944: Requires existing facilities and operations to comply with new environmental protection and public health standards. Amendment 6945: Prohibits lease buyouts, including wind leases off of California’s coast. Amendment 6946: Prohibits offshore oil and gas leasing off the West Coast. ###

WASHINGTON, D.C. — Today, U.S. Senators Alex Padilla, Adam Schiff, (both D-Calif.), Bill Cassidy (R-La.), and Todd Young (R-Ind.) introduced the bipartisan Medicaid Inclusion and Non-Discrimination (MIND) Act , a targeted, protections-first bill to help adults in a mental health crisis more easily get care in small, community-based facilities. The bill would allow Medicaid to cover inpatient psychiatric care at certain facilities with 17 to 32 beds that must also meet strong new federal patient protection standards. Since Medicaid’s enactment in 1965, the Institution for Mental Diseases (IMD) exclusion has barred federal Medicaid payment for care provided to adults in mental health facilities with more than 16 beds. It is the only provision in federal Medicaid law that denies payment for medically necessary care solely because of the illness being treated. A Medicaid enrollee hospitalized for cancer, heart disease, or diabetes is covered. The same enrollee hospitalized for schizophrenia in a 17-bed facility is not. Fewer than 8% of psychiatric hospitals fall at or under the 16-bed limit, leaving the vast majority of inpatient mental health settings off limits to Medicaid patients. This bill would extend coverage only to small, community-scale facilities, preserving the strong federal preference for community-based treatment while ending the payment rule that punishes patients for their diagnosis. The MIND Act does not repeal the IMD exclusion but instead updates it to better reflect current needs in our communities. “Americans in a mental health crisis deserve the same access to care as patients facing other serious illness,” said Senator Padilla . “Right now, an outdated payment rule keeps Medicaid from covering care at many small, community-based mental health facilities, leaving patients to wait in emergency rooms or go without treatment. Our bipartisan bill is a targeted fix with strong patient protections to help close that gap and get people the care they need closer to home.” “Affordable access to inpatient psychiatric care is already limited, and the current IMD exclusion has caused shortages of psychiatric beds and treatment services across our communities,” said Senator Schiff . “I’m proud to partner with Senators Padilla, Young, and Cassidy to increase the IMD exclusion from 16 to 32 beds — overcoming a key barrier to increasing access to inpatient psychiatric care and easing the financial strain on California’s counties who have been left bearing the costs.” “Communities need more tools to effectively treat severe mental illness. This legislation will empower states and community providers to give patients the care they need and deserve,” said Dr. Cassidy. “I am pleased to have worked on this legislation to make treatment of severe mental illness more accessible and affordable for the patient.” “Many Hoosiers struggling with serious mental illness face unnecessary barriers to receiving the care they need,” said Senator Young . “Our bill would remove outdated federal restrictions that limit access to mental health treatment—particularly for our homeless population—and allow community-based facilities greater flexibility to serve patients. This commonsense reform will help expand treatment options and strengthen mental health care services in communities across Indiana.” Covered facilities must meet requirements on patient rights, restraint and seclusion limits, utilization review, and discharge planning. Specifically, the MIND Act would ensure community-scale medical facilities guarantee : Informed consent and patient rights: Patients (and their guardians or conservators) may refuse any treatment or experimental procedure absent a court order, and receive an individualized written treatment plan with clear discharge criteria, updated at least every six months; Strict limits on restraint and seclusion: Never for coercion, discipline, convenience, or retaliation; no standing or as needed orders; full documentation of every order, every shift; Independent accountability: Utilization review of every continued stay at least every 90 days, unannounced state oversight visits; and A path back to the community: Confidential access to patient advocates and attorneys, retaliation free grievance rights, and dedicated discharge case management to return each patient safely and quickly to the community of their choice, with annual state reporting to HHS on lengths of stay, restraint and seclusion, and discharge delays. “Counties finance and operate much of the nation’s local behavioral health and crisis infrastructure. The outdated 16-bed Medicaid Institutions for Mental Disease (IMD) cap limits our ability to deliver timely inpatient care and leaves local jails and emergency rooms to fill the gap,” said National Association of Counties Executive Director Matthew Chase . “Sen. Alex Padilla’s MIND Act is a meaningful step forward, and we strongly support its effort to expand Medicaid coverage to facilities with up to 32 beds while protecting patients and strengthening discharge transitions back into our communities.” Padilla has championed legislation to guarantee healthcare regardless of income. In July, Padilla joined Senator Andy Kim (D-N.J.) in introducing the MediKids Act , monumental legislation guaranteeing healthcare to all children in America from birth to age 26. Padilla also reintroduced the Health Equity and Accountability Act (HEAA) of 2026 , bicameral legislation that would address health disparities among racial and ethnic minorities as well as women, the LGBTQ+ community, rural populations, and socioeconomically disadvantaged communities across the United States. Last year, Padilla joined Senator Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and over 100 lawmakers in reintroducing the Medicare for All Act , legislation that would guarantee healthcare as a fundamental human right to all people in the United States regardless of income or background. Full transcript is available below: Mr. President, two weeks ago, the American people made history. An estimated 124 million Americans voted in this year’s midterm elections, the second highest turnout rate for a midterm in more than a century. Now, a new generation of leaders, who better reflect the diversity and promise of our nation, is headed to Washington, D.C., into State Capitols across the country. California, my home state, elected its first Latino governor. The state of Georgia elected the first Black woman as governor, the state of Texas will have its first Latina governor. The state of New Mexico will have its first Native American woman governor, and here in this chamber, we are about to welcome the first Muslim United States senator, the first Black senator from the state of Mississippi since 1881, and the first Native American woman to serve in the United States Senate. All historic victories made possible by the American people who showed up and exercised their right to vote. Now, for months, I predicted that voters would hold this Administration accountable. This historic turnout rate was certainly inspired by the conditions that the American people are living in. Voters sought to hold this Administration accountable for economic policies that are making life increasingly unaffordable. For the corruption, the self-dealing, and the relentless attacks on our institutions. For a reckless and unauthorized and costly war with Iran. And for a cruel mass deportation campaign that has terrorized communities and taken the lives of both immigrants and United States citizens alike. And two weeks ago, it’s exactly what voters did, and the message they sent could not be any louder and could not be any clearer. The people want an end to the chaos, an end to the corruption, and an end to the cruelty. They want affordability. They want accountability. And above all, they want a government that works for them, not against them. Now I know Democrats have heard this message loud and clear, and we intend to deliver. But before looking too far ahead, before we start debating about what the next Congress will prioritize and take action on, it’s important that we acknowledge and reflect on what it took for Americans to make their voices heard this year, because if there’s a fundamental lesson to take from these midterm elections, it’s that our democracy is not self-executing. It depends on Americans showing up to defend it, on elections officials ensuring that every eligible vote is counted, and on people wanting to stand up when the right to vote is threatened. So let’s be clear: these midterms were under threat from the very beginning of this Trump Administration. Donald Trump and his MAGA allies spent nearly two years using the power of the presidency to undermine confidence in our elections and seeking to make it harder for the American people to vote. They spread baseless lies about election integrity. They threatened to deploy federal law enforcement and troops to polling locations. They attacked mail-in voting and pressured states to turn over confidential voter rolls. They gutted the Voting Rights Act and pushed aggressive racial and partisan gerrymandering in an attempt to hold on to power. And when states like California stood up to Trump, Trump’s Justice Department filed lawsuits seeking to throw out ballots from eligible voters based on unreliable data, but Americans saw right through it, and they refused to be deterred by this Administration’s attacks. Eligible Americans registered to vote. And then they voted. They voted early. They voted by mail. They returned their ballots to drop boxes, and they made voices heard in record numbers. As one of President Trump’s own advisers told CNN, the election was, quote, “essentially too big to rig.” Think about that. Too many Americans showed up. Too many people made their voices heard. The margins of victory was so big – any attempt to slow down the count, throw out ballots, try to, you know, twist the rules to try to eke out some victories when they were losing, wasn’t going to happen. And the record number of people who turned out weren’t alone. An unprecedented coalition of civil society organizations, voting rights groups, and state and local elections officials pushed back on the Administration’s attempts to interfere. And Democrats on the Rules Committee, together with Leader Schumer’s Election Protection Task Force – and I want to give Leader Schumer the credit he deserves for convening this task force and investing in it. We also worked together to help create the Senate’s first Election Observer program. We trained more than 100 Senate staff in election law and procedure, and deployed more than 60 staff members to more than a dozen states to monitor polling places, the vote counting, canvassing process. It was important to oversee to ensure accountability. And for the staff that served, and for the staff of the Rules Committee who developed and successfully implemented this program: thank you, thank you, thank you for your service, and thank you to all the members of the broad coalition that came together to defend our democracy and our access to the ballot. Your efforts made a difference. Voter suppression executive orders were stopped. Courts rejected the Justice Department’s attempts to obtain state voter roll data 28 times. And in the states of California and Washington, courts blocked the Administration’s efforts to interfere with the counting of eligible, lawful ballots. Now, these victories sound like common sense, but these victories matter. They show what is possible when people stand together to defend our democracy. But the fight is far from over. One election may be behind us, but the next election is less than two years away, and there’s still too many barriers keeping too many eligible Americans from being able to vote, like the backlog of 600,000 voter registration applications that the state of Texas failed to process on a timely basis. The voters in Tarrant County, Texas, for example, who waited in line for hours after officials slashed a third of the polling places in that county. That’s unacceptable. The young voters in North Carolina who marched for miles along highways to cast ballots because early voting locations at historically Black colleges were closed. Thousands of voters were purged in Mississippi based on unreliable credit agency address data, leading to a surge in affidavits, otherwise known as provisional ballots, two thirds of which were rejected, just in Hinds County alone. We need to shore up our elections by giving state and local officials the resources they need to run secure, and accessible, and efficient elections. And we need to ensure that every eligible American’s access to the ballot box by expanding automatic voter registration and vote by mail, and preventing eligible voters from being wrongly purged from the voter rolls. There’s plenty of states across the country, not just California, where I believe we have the gold standard, that have implemented these policies, these new laws, the best practices, if you will, to maintain safe and secure elections, but making sure they are free and fair by modernizing elections and giving voters more opportunity to be able to participate in our democracy. It’s so fundamental. We also need fair redistricting, and we need to get big money out of politics and permanently put our elections back in the hands of the people by overturning the Citizens United decision. That is the unfinished work of this democracy that still remains ahead of us. And, Mr. President, if I have the privilege of serving as chair of the Rules Committee in the next Congress, that’s the kind of work that I look forward to taking on. Mr. President, the American people delivered resounding results and historic firsts of this year’s election because they were sending a message. With the sanctity of our elections threatened, and so much on the line for working families, the American people showed up in record numbers to demand change. They demanded accountability from an Administration that tried to undermine the right to vote, tried to keep the American people from having their voices heard. The same Administration that has put its own interest ahead of theirs. The people demanded an end to the chaos and the corruption that have gripped our country these last two years, and they demanded a government make life more affordable and gives working families a fair shot at a better future. So, with the election now behind us, we can say the American people have done their part, and now it’s time for us to do ours. Thank you, Mr. President. I yield the floor. ###

WASHINGTON, D.C. — Today, U.S. Senators Alex Padilla and Adam Schiff (both D-Calif.) announced that their bicameral and bipartisan bills to promote Tribal management of over 800 acres of land in California passed in the Senate and House of Representatives. The Pit River Land Transfer Act and Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians Land Transfer Act now head to President Trump’s desk to be signed into law. “For too long, California’s Tribal nations have been denied the right to manage and preserve their ancestral lands. The historic passage of these two bills represents a key step toward righting our historical wrongs,” said Senator Padilla. “Restoring tribal land to its original owners preserves traditions, strengthens communities, and supports ecological health across California. I am proud to support the Pit River Tribe and the Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians and I am grateful for the bipartisan, bicameral support that made these land transfers possible.” “For generations, California’s tribes have fought to rightfully restore their ancestral homelands and preserve the culture of their ancestors,” said Senator Schiff . “I am proud Congress has passed our legislation to help the Pit River Tribe and Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians reclaim their cultural lands and promote tribal sovereignty.” Pit River Land Transfer Act This bill would transfer 557 acres of federal land administered by the United States Forest Service to the Department of the Interior to be held in trust for the Pit River Tribe. The Tribe has been actively trying to acquire this land through various governmental processes for over a decade. However, they have experienced a series of delays that have added years to the process. The late Representative Doug LaMalfa (R-Calif.-01) led companion legislation in the House of Representatives, which is now led by Representative James Gallagher (R-Calif.-01). “Doug LaMalfa was a tireless advocate for the North State, and returning this land to the Pit River Tribe was a cause he believed in,” said Representative Gallagher . “I’m honored to carry his work forward and grateful to Senator Padilla for his partnership in moving this legislation through the Senate. The Tribe has waited more than a decade for this, and it’s encouraging to see Republicans and Democrats working together to get it across the finish line.” “For the Pit River Tribe, Four Corners is more than a parcel of land. It is a place that connects our ancestors, our history, and our future,” said Pit River Tribe Chairman Yatch Bamford . “Passage of this legislation brings us closer to caring for this land as its Stewards, preserving a site central to our people’s struggle for justice, and creating a place where future generations can learn our history. We thank Senator Padilla for his leadership and tireless work in securing passage of this bill, and Senator Schiff for his support. We are also deeply grateful to the late Congressman Doug LaMalfa for his leadership and work to advance this legislation. Their commitments to our Tribe made this milestone possible, as we work toward a future rooted in our culture and shaped by our people.” The Pit River Tribe consist of 11 autonomous bands traditionally inhabiting the area surrounding the Pit River and its tributaries. They are known for their deep spiritual connection to the land, with a rich cultural heritage centered around fishing, hunting, and seasonal gatherings. The proposed land to be transferred is known as the Four Corners Property, located in Shasta County. The Tribe has strong cultural and historical connections to the Four Corners, and they view it as a central landmark of their ancestral lands. In October 1970, members of the Tribe erected a Quonset hut on the Four Corners, staking a peaceful, yet firm claim. That month, over 100 sheriff’s deputies, federal marshals, and forest rangers ordered the occupants to evacuate the property, which eventually resulted in violence and the hospitalization of several Tribal members. Full text of the Pit River Land Transfer Act is available here . Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians Land Transfer Act This bill would place approximately 80 acres of land currently managed by the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) into trust for the Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians, a federally recognized Tribe whose reservation is located near Placerville in the western Sierra Nevada foothills. The bill would also place into trust 185 acres of fee land already owned by the Tribe. Representative Tom McClintock (R-Calif.-05) is leading companion legislation in the House of Representatives. “The Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians survived near annihilation during the Spanish and Gold Rush eras to become a prosperous and integral part of El Dorado County. I am honored to carry this legislation that will continue their progress and contributions to their posterity and to our community into the years ahead,” said Representative McClintock . “This legislation is about our homeland and the future we are building for our children and grandchildren,” said Chairwoman Regina Cuellar . “Its passage brings us closer to securing these lands for our people and strengthening our ability to care for them for generations to come. We thank Senators Padilla and Schiff and Congressman McClintock for their leadership and work to secure passage of this legislation. We are deeply grateful for their commitment to our Tribe and support for our future.” The Tribe’s current trust land base is just 317 acres and their reservation access was significantly disrupted decades ago when Highway 50 was constructed across their only entrance. While the Tribe has since invested in an off-ramp to restore access, their existing land remains insufficient to meet the needs of their citizens. This bill would place BLM land into trust for the Tribe to maintain it for open space and fire risk management. By enabling the Tribe to place their existing fee land into trust, the bill would help the Tribe build much-needed housing. Full text of the Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians Land Transfer Act is available here . Padilla is a strong advocate for restoring Tribal ownership of ancestral lands. Last week, Padilla and Schiff introduced legislation to transfer over 800 acres of federal land into trust for the Barona Band of Mission Indians. In July, Padilla testified at a Senate Committee on Indian Affairs hearing to advocate for critical water investments for California Tribes. In March, Padilla and Schiff introduced legislation to transfer 860 acres of land from the BLM into trust for the Pechanga Band of Indians. ###

WASHINGTON, D.C. — Today, U.S. Senators Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee’s Immigration Subcommittee, and Jacky Rosen (D-Nev.) introduced the Travel Without Fear Act , a bill to limit the ability of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to broadly conduct civil immigration operations at or near airports without a judicial warrant related to a felony criminal conviction. The bill would also ban information sharing between ICE and the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) for civil immigration enforcement actions unless they have a judicial warrant for a specific target or is for the purposes of maintaining trusted traveler programs. In the last year, there has been an increase in violent ICE civil enforcement operations at airports across America. This includes a recent incident in which a student at UC Berkeley was arrested at San Francisco International Airport (SFO) and detained in an ICE facility in California City for more than a week. According to their own reports , ICE recorded the highest number of administrative arrests in ICE’s history. Earlier this year, Padilla conducted an oversight visit to the California City facility to learn firsthand of the concerns surrounding the condition of detained individuals at this facility amid the Trump Administration’s mass detention and deportation campaign. “ICE is out of control, and these are bare minimum standards for reining it in: officers who are visibly identifiable, as my VISIBLE Act requires, protections for travelers’ personal information, and a check for pending applications before arrests,” said Senator Padilla. “These safeguards protect everyone involved – travelers, officers, and the public. It’s commonsense and responsible.” “ICE should not be allowed to operate recklessly and aggressively in our communities – putting lives and livelihoods at risk. We’ve even seen ICE operating with impunity inside airports, sowing chaos and fear, and further disrupting Nevada’s tourism economy,” said Senator Rosen . “That’s why I’m introducing this bill to prohibit ICE from conducting civil enforcement operations at airports without a judicial warrant, and to set clear guidelines for their conduct when they have one.” The legislation would further require ICE officers to ensure that targets for arrest or detention are not within a period of authorized stay, prohibit ICE from accessing passenger data without a warrant, require ICE to notify airports and airlines in advance of any enforcement action, and require updates to the online database that tracks detainee locations for their families and attorneys within six hours of a detainee’s change in custody. In addition to Padilla and Rosen, the bill is cosponsored by Senator Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.). Padilla has been a leader in holding the Trump Administration accountable for its cruel and reckless mass deportation agenda. Last week, Padilla and Senator Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) demanded answers over the detention of an eight-year-old Haitian child who lost Temporary Protected Status during a routine immigration check in. Last month, Padilla pressed Department of Homeland Security (DHS) officials over reports of increased ICE enforcement activity in Mendota and across California. In September, Padilla called on DHS to end immigration enforcement activity around San Diego County schools and educational institutions. In August, Padilla called out the Trump Administration’s continued abuses of power and demanded accountability. In June, Padilla sounded the alarm over the significant increase in deaths among detainees in ICE custody since January 2025. In April, Padilla and Schiff launched an inquiry into data sharing by TSA and ICE officials relating to the arrest and removal of Angelina Lopez-Jimenez and her child at SFO. Padilla has also repeatedly conducted oversight visits to immigration detention facilities and holding centers across California to examine conditions firsthand and demand accountability from federal officials. His visits include facilities in California City , Otay Mesa , San Francisco International Airport , Downtown Los Angeles , Sacramento , San Diego , and McFarland . Legislation now heads to President’s desk to become law WASHINGTON, D.C. — Today, U.S. Senator Alex Padilla (D-Calif.) and U.S. Representative Tom McClintock (R-Calif.-05) announced their Ackerson Meadow Land Interchange Act , to facilitate a land exchange between the National Park Service (NPS) and the U.S. Forest Service (USFS) in the Sierra Nevada, advanced through the Senate and now heads to President Trump’s desk to be signed into law. This legislation would transfer 160 acres of Stanislaus National Forest land to the NPS to be managed as part of Yosemite National Park and transfer 170 acres of Yosemite National Park land to the USFS to be managed as part of Stanislaus National Forest. The land in the exchange is known as Ackerson Meadow. “Ackerson Meadow is one of the most critical wildlife corridors in our state, yet the current configuration of the region puts habitat conservation at risk,” said Senator Padilla . “This land transfer is a simple and beneficial exchange that will help protect endangered wildlife, mitigate wildfire threats, and sustain our rural economy. I’m proud to get the legislation over the finish line, and I will continue fighting for our public lands and endangered wildlife.” “This legislation addresses a familiar problem in federal land management in the Sierra Nevada: the checkerboard of boundary lines that makes land management disjointed and inefficient,” said Representative McClintock . “The bill consolidates land jurisdictions between the National Park System and the National Forest System, without increasing the federal footprint. Ackerson Meadow supports livestock grazing operations that have been part of the history and economy of the region. These operations are essential for brush control and fire suppression, maintaining meadow conditions and sustaining the rural economy that depends on the productive use of these lands. Federal agencies, conservation organizations, and local ranchers have worked together to improve the meadow while maintaining grazing opportunities. The land exchange will make that cooperative approach easier by eliminating the confusion caused by split jurisdiction.” In 2016, the Trust for Public Land bought a 400-acre parcel of land known as Ackerson Meadow and gifted it to Yosemite National Park. However, while much of Ackerson Meadow is stunning and meets the criteria for being in a National Park, it is almost completely surrounded by the Stanislaus National Forest with very little contiguous border to the park itself. Since the current configuration of land ownership is not conducive to efficient land management, an interagency land exchange is supported by the USFS, NPS, and local stakeholders, including a permittee who runs a large cattle operation near Ackerson Meadow. Full text of the bill is available here . A map of the land exchange is here . ###
