WASHINGTON, D.C. — U.S. Senator Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Immigration Subcommittee, and Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-Ill.) demanded Department of Justice (DOJ) Inspector General Don Berthiaume open an investigation into the concerning activities detailed in a recent whistleblower disclosure alleging that the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), under White House and DOJ leadership’s direction, opened unconstitutional investigations into Los Angeles protestors solely for exercising their First Amendment rights. The letter was co-signed by Senators Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Cory Booker (D-N.J.), Mazie Hirono (D-Hawaii), Adam Schiff (D-Calif.), and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.). In their letter, the Senators highlighted the whistleblower’s allegations that, in one incident, the White House instructed FBI Director Kash Patel to have the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office open an investigation into the protesters solely based on First Amendment activity, violating agency policy and protestors’ constitutional rights. “These investigations were opened following increased protests against aggressive immigration enforcement actions by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) in the Los Angeles area,” wrote the Senators . “The Disclosure states that no actual or potential national security threat or federal criminal activity existed on which to predicate investigating the protesters. The Disclosure also alleges that the investigations pulled FBI employees and resources away from active cases involving drug trafficking, violent crime, and transnational criminal organizations. Although the whistleblower and others at the Los Angeles Field Office raised concerns that these investigations unlawfully targeted individuals for exercising their First Amendment rights, the investigations allegedly proceeded nevertheless.” In addition to the investigation, the Senators urged Berthiaume to take immediate action to address potential misconduct within the FBI to prevent any additional wrongdoing. “We request that you open an independent investigation into the troubling allegations detailed in the Disclosure, which describes DOJ and FBI leadership directing personnel to initiate investigations based solely on First Amendment activity under political pressure,” wrote the Senators. “We further request that you investigate whether and to what extent the FBI’s Domestic Investigations and Operations Guide—and any provisions concerning First Amendment activity therein — have been amended during Director Patel’s tenure.” “Given the serious questions the Disclosure raises about the misuse of federal law enforcement resources and the legality and constitutionality of these directives to FBI personnel, please provide regular updates on the status of your investigation to the leadership of the Senate Committee on the Judiciary,” the Senators concluded . “If the Attorney General refuses to cooperate with an audit or investigation into these allegations, please notify us immediately.” The whistleblower’s disclosure follows a chilling pattern in which the Administration has pursued Trump’s baseless claims at the expense of Americans’ safety. A separate, recent whistleblower disclosure alleges Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) leadership abruptly diverted USCIS Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate immigration officers from their national security-related duties and directed them instead to use illegal procedures and questionable data to identify purported “unlawful voters,” and create federal law enforcement records against them, including naturalized U.S. citizens. The Administration also redirected Homeland Security Investigations analysts from their typical work on criminal matters and to a so-called “tiger team” for the sole purpose of investigating, surveilling, and detaining students and other individuals based solely on their political opinions. Padilla has fought to hold the Trump Administration accountable. In January, Padilla and Senator Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) introduced a bill to reaffirm the right to free speech and safeguard Americans from politically motivated harassment and prosecution. The whistleblower disclosure is available here . Full text of the letter is available here and below: Dear Inspector General Berthiaume: On October 5, 2026, the Senate Committee on the Judiciary received the attached protected whistleblower disclosure (the Disclosure) through the Government Accountability Project. It reveals serious allegations that the Department of Justice (DOJ) and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) opened unconstitutional investigations of protesters engaged in protected First Amendment activity. According to the Disclosure, the White House, DOJ leadership, and FBI leadership directed the Los Angeles FBI Field Office to open two different investigations in 2025 based solely on individuals’ participation in First Amendment activity—in violation of agency policy and protesters’ constitutional rights. These investigations were opened following increased protests against aggressive immigration enforcement actions by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) in the Los Angeles area. The Disclosure states that no actual or potential national security threat or federal criminal activity existed on which to predicate investigating the protesters. The Disclosure also alleges that the investigations pulled FBI employees and resources away from active cases involving drug trafficking, violent crime, and transnational criminal organizations. Although the whistleblower and others at the Los Angeles Field Office raised concerns that these investigations unlawfully targeted individuals for exercising their First Amendment rights, the investigations allegedly proceeded nevertheless. The Disclosure includes credible whistleblower allegations of wrongdoing and abuse of power by DOJ and FBI leadership in two instances: (1) Then-DOJ Acting Deputy Attorney General Emil Bove directed the Los Angeles Field Office to open an investigation into any anti-ICE and CBP protestors demonstrating at federal buildings in Los Angeles without identifying any clearly articulated actual or potential national security threat, criminal activity, or vulnerability to such threats and activities; and (2) After President Trump reportedly viewed a TikTok video of protestors in Alhambra, California that alerted neighbors about ICE’s presence and advised them of their legal rights, the White House instructed FBI Director Kash Patel to direct the Los Angeles Field Office to initiate an investigation into the protestors. We request that you open an independent investigation into the troubling allegations detailed in the Disclosure, which describes DOJ and FBI leadership directing personnel to initiate investigations based solely on First Amendment activity under political pressure. We further request that you investigate whether and to what extent the FBI’s Domestic Investigations and Operations Guide—and any provisions concerning First Amendment activity therein—have been amended during Director Patel’s tenure. Based on the allegations in the Disclosure and due to the risk that the FBI may continue to violate agency policies and unlawfully target individuals exercising their constitutional rights, we believe a management alert may be appropriate to address this alleged misconduct immediately and prevent any additional wrongdoing or misuse of FBI personnel and resources while your office’s investigation is ongoing. Given the serious questions the Disclosure raises about the misuse of federal law enforcement resources and the legality and constitutionality of these directives to FBI personnel, please provide regular updates on the status of your investigation to the leadership of the Senate Committee on the Judiciary. If the Attorney General refuses to cooperate with an audit or investigation into these allegations, please notify us immediately. Thank you for your attention to this important matter. ###

Key Democratic Committee Leaders to Tech CEOs: “We strongly urge you to enhance—not reduce—your election security efforts in the final days before the 2026 midterms” WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Senators Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), Ranking Member of the Senate Rules and Administration Committee, Mark R. Warner (D-Va.), Vice Chairman of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, along with U.S. Representatives Jim Himes (D-Conn.-04), Ranking Member of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, and Joe Morelle (D-N.Y.-25), Ranking Member of the House Administration Committee, urged top executives of the largest technology companies to ensure their platforms and tools help protect the integrity of our elections and support free, fair, and secure elections. In their letter, the lawmakers underscored the need for social media and technology companies to do their part to promote election security. They outlined the potential risk to elections created by the spread of false information through social media platforms and artificial intelligence. “Your platforms play a significant and important role in sharing, disseminating, and in some cases generating information about those elections,” wrote the lawmakers. “Much of the United States—and the world—searches for and receives information from American search engines, American chatbots, and American social media platforms. These connections create opportunities for Americans to come together and debate important topics and share information. But they also create vectors for foreign adversaries and domestic actors to easily and quickly reach—and manipulate—large audiences.” The lawmakers reminded the CEOs that many of their companies committed to ensuring they were not complicit in harming elections or hampering the ability of Americans to vote. They explained that, while many of these companies have committed to authenticating and labeling digital media and adopted policies to boost the most reliable voting and election information, there have been inconsistencies in the efficacy and application of these policies. “Unfortunately, there are concerning signs of backsliding on some of your commitments to protecting elections from misuse of your products. These signs are particularly alarming because they come at a time when the capabilities of malign actors are growing in scale and sophistication and our elections are under attack from multiple directions,” wrote the lawmakers. “Public reporting indicates that Russia continues to undermine confidence in U.S. elections through disinformation campaigns executed directly on many of your platforms; though such efforts clearly violate your terms of service, some of your companies have not quickly or consistently removed such content.” The lawmakers further explained that their social media platforms and AI tools can quickly generate, execute and disseminate influence campaigns that used to take hundreds of hours of labor. As Americans increasingly turn to AI tools to inform themselves about political candidates, ballot issues, and the logistics of voting, AI tools could be used to spread inaccurate, outdated, manipulated, or biased information. “Equally alarming is that some of your AI chatbots have an unacceptably high error rate when responding to queries about election and voting processes, subjecting users to confusing or inaccurate answers that could result in voter disenfranchisement. And some of your content removal and fact-checking policies are woefully insufficient or even nonexistent, allowing false, manipulated, and misleading content to continue to circulate on your platforms unchecked,” the lawmakers continued. The lawmakers recommended a list of concrete actions the companies could take, including removing all demonstrably false information related to election and voting logistics once they find it, using independent fact checkers, regularly updating automated tools to review and remove or reduce the reach of false election-related content, and directing all users to authoritative election-related resources. They also urged the companies to ensure AI-generated responses to questions about election and voting logistics are sourced from state and local election offices and trusted news organizations. “Again, we strongly urge you to enhance—not reduce—your election security efforts in the final days before the 2026 midterms and to maintain strong efforts in this area on an ongoing basis ahead of future elections as well,” the lawmakers concluded . As Ranking Member of the Senate Rules Committee with oversight over federal elections and California’s former Secretary of State, Padilla has been a vocal leader in protecting our elections. Earlier this month, Padilla and Senator Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) pressed the top executives of the largest social media companies about their plans to combat misinformation and disinformation on their platforms ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. In August, Padilla and Senator Mark Warner (D-Va.) called for prediction market companies to take immediate action to protect election integrity and end relationships with paid influencers on their platforms spreading election disinformation. The full letter is available here and below. Dear Mr. Narayen, Mr. Pichai, Mr. Amodei, Mr. Rombach, Mr. Schneider, Mr. Sakhnini, Mr. Staniszewski, Mr. Shapero, Mr. Zuckerberg, Mr. Nadella, Mr. Holz, Mr. Mensch, Mr. Altman, Mr. Srinivas, Mr. Ready, Mr. Huffman, Mr. Laskin, Mr. Pavlovski, Mr. Spiegel, Mr. Musk, Mr. Akkaraju, Mr. Durov, Mrs. Murati, Mr. Presser, and Mr. McGurn, We write to urge you to adopt policies and programs that ensure your platforms contribute to, and do not detract from, the effort to ensure that America’s elections are free, fair, and secure. As the CEOs of America’s largest technology companies, you are aware of the great responsibility that your companies hold in America’s elections. Your platforms play a significant and important role in sharing, disseminating, and in some cases generating information about those elections. Much of the United States—and the world—searches for and receives information from American search engines, American chatbots, and American social media platforms. These connections create opportunities for Americans to come together and debate important topics and share information. But they also create vectors for foreign adversaries and domestic actors to easily and quickly reach—and manipulate—large audiences. Moreover, American companies’ AI offerings offer both substantial benefits and substantial risks. Your tools can quickly generate, execute, and disseminate entire influence campaigns. While it previously would take hundreds of manhours to achieve such effects, your tools speed and streamline efforts to create material that are inaccurate or false, but nevertheless convincing. Increasingly, some American voters turn to AI tools to research candidates and ballot issues and seek information about voting logistics, increasing the risk of exposure to inaccuracies, outdated or manipulated information, or biased summaries. Many of your companies have demonstrated a commitment over the past decade to ensuring that your platforms are not used to harm elections or hamper the ability of Americans to vote. After the 2016 elections, many of your companies turned particular focus to identifying and eliminating coordinated inauthentic behavior on your platforms and establishing searchable archives for election ads. With the rise of powerful generative AI tools, your companies further committed to authenticating and labeling digital media, including by joining the Coalition for Content Provenance & Authenticity (C2PA) and signing the Tech Accord to Combat Deceptive Use of AI in 2024 Elections. Many of your companies have also adopted policies seeking to increase the odds that your users are exposed to only the most authoritative and reliable voting and election information. We believe maintaining and enhancing these kinds of commitments is more important than ever heading into the final days of the 2026 midterm election cycle. Unfortunately, there are concerning signs of backsliding on some of your commitments to protecting elections from misuse of your products. These signs are particularly alarming because they come at a time when the capabilities of malign actors are growing in scale and sophistication and our elections are under attack from multiple directions. Despite many of your companies having policies prohibiting deception and requiring the labeling of AI-generated content, there have been demonstrated inconsistencies regarding the effectiveness and applicability of your policies. In many cases, some of your social media platforms and AI tools still allow for the creation and/or dissemination of false, synthetic, misleading, or inauthentic election content in direct violation of your policies. Public reporting indicates that Russia continues to undermine confidence in U.S. elections through disinformation campaigns executed directly on many of your platforms; though such efforts clearly violate your terms of service, some of your companies have not quickly or consistently removed such content. Equally alarming is that some of your AI chatbots have an unacceptably high error rate when responding to queries about election and voting processes, subjecting users to confusing or inaccurate answers that could result in voter disenfranchisement. And some of your content removal and fact-checking policies are woefully insufficient or even nonexistent, allowing false, manipulated, and misleading content to continue to circulate on your platforms unchecked. In the past, the Federal Trade Commission has notably pursued enforcement actions against companies that don’t live up to the self-regulatory commitments they make, including in a 2012 case against Google for failing to follow the National Advertising Initiative code of conduct. Information related to election and voting logistics—a category that includes registration deadlines, polling hours and locations, requirements about voter ID, rules for mail or provisional voting and ballots, and voter eligibility—is information that is integral to the functioning of our democracy. When objectively false information about election administration is introduced and disseminated with the intent to deceive or to discourage prospective voters, your companies must have robust and consistently applied rules to differentiate that misinformation from ordinary political speech about elections and to take steps to remove that misinformation. We continue to strongly encourage you to take the actions and adopt the best practices outlined in Senator Warner’s March 2026 letter on anticipating, identifying, and countering malicious manipulated media. These best practices are important steps to protecting vulnerable communities, public trust, and democratic institutions. We also encourage you to adopt specific policies and actions regarding election-related content. To the extent that your company offers social media or other content access or distribution platforms, we strongly encourage you to take the following actions to keep your platforms free from coordinated inauthentic behavior and election-related misinformation and disinformation: Immediately remove all demonstrably false information related to election and voting logistics upon becoming aware of it—including information about where and how to register to vote, and where and how to vote. Support dedicated reporting tools on your platforms for election officials to report examples of false election information. Improve the speed by which your tools detect and remove false information related to voting logistics and political and election-related violence. o When such tools are used to detect false, misleading, and inauthentic content, ensure that the tools are kept updated, and that their findings are promptly subject to human review and action to remove violative content. Utilize independent fact checkers in addition to internal fact-checking teams and regularly updated automated tools to review and remove, or at least reduce the reach, impressions, and discoverability of, false, misleading, or inauthentic election-related content. Engage independent media and civil society organizations to assist in efforts to verify media, generate authenticated media, and educate the public. Notify users when they have engaged with election-related content that has subsequently been determined to be false, misleading, or inauthentic. Affirmatively direct all users to authoritative election-related resources, especially if users were determined to have engaged with false, misleading, or inauthentic election-related content. Immediately remove all content advocating for violence of any kind upon becoming aware of it, but particularly content advocating political and/or election-related violence. Publish regular reports detailing efforts to identify and remove false election-related information, election-related misinformation and disinformation, election and political violence, and coordinated inauthentic behavior. To the extent your company offers generative AI products, we strongly encourage you to take the following actions to keep your AI systems and tools safe as they engage with and generate election-related information: Ensure that AI-generated responses to questions about election and voting logistics pull only from highly authoritative sources and do not pull from social media platforms or other user-generated content. Authoritative resources should be limited to state and local election offices and top trusted news organizations, as well as civil society organizations aggregating content from these other authoritative and reliable sources. Provide additional resources to pre-deployment guardrail testing for AI-generated election-related content, as well as ongoing reviewing of model performance. Strengthen guardrails to prevent AI systems from responding to queries with material that can be used in election disinformation campaigns. Implement continuous auditing until the November federal elections, and for an appropriate time as ballot counting, litigation, or challenges to the results remain ongoing, for accuracy and objectiveness in AI-generated responses to election-related questions, including mechanisms by which users can report inaccurate answers. Incorporate disclaimers and flags in AI-generated responses if election and voting logistics may be outdated, and direct users to authoritative resources. Provide inline citations and links for all election-related information provided in an AI-generated response. Encourage users to independently verify AI-generated answers to questions about election and voting by reviewing authoritative and reliable resources. Ensure that all AI-generated images and videos are consistently clearly labeled and can be identified as AI-generated content both by the human eye and by technology-based detection tools. Ensure that election-related responses provided in languages other than English are accurate and reliable. Many of you have announced content partnerships with highly reliable sources to ensure that your AI and social media platforms only surface the most accurate and reliable information related to election and voting logistics and election results. We strongly support this practice and encourage you to ensure that your platforms properly identify and curate the authoritative and reliable resources from which they pull from on election-related topics to avoid sharing outdated, inaccurate, unreliable, or otherwise incorrect information on this critical topic area that you cannot afford to get wrong. In addition, we urge you to be mindful of Spanish and other foreign language content, which plays a large and important role in the U.S. electorate but often receives less attention and response than online English-language election misinformation. We also encourage you to be transparent about the efforts that your companies are making on these fronts. Public reporting indicates that in recent years, several of your companies have conducted layoffs, including of personnel on the trust and safety teams responsible for ensuring your platforms’ integrity when it comes to election topics. Firing such personnel after there has been demonstrated evidence and indicators of orchestrated and coordinate foreign misinformation operations exposes your platform to various integrity threats and is cause for serious concern. Particularly as the 2026 midterm elections are officially underway, your companies should be increasing the staffing and capabilities of your respective trust and safety teams, especially those teams responsible for avoiding platform exploitation relating to election topics. Refusing to grow and expand your election integrity teams—and even shrinking these teams—does not support your stated commitments to countering harmful election content and suggests to bad actors that your policies are not enforceable. Finally, third-party researchers play a critical role in studying and producing independent reviews of social media platforms and AI systems and tools, particularly as it pertains to auditing the effectiveness of your trust and safety policies. Your companies should collaborate with third-party researchers by granting them access to your products and data, including data on how users are engaging with your platforms on election-related issues, and allow for the testing of your platforms and AI tools. Again, we strongly urge you to enhance—not reduce—your election security efforts in the final days before the 2026 midterms and to maintain strong efforts in this area on an ongoing basis ahead of future elections as well. We thank you for your attention to these important measures and we look forward to hearing about your efforts in these areas. Sincerely,

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, Senator Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), Ranking Member of the Senate Committee on Rules and Administration, and Ranking Member Joe Morelle (D-N.Y.-25), the top Democrat on the Committee on House Administration, sent a joint oversight letter to Acting Deputy Attorney General R. Trent McCotter after the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) sued California’s Secretary of State and Los Angeles County’s Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk with no legal basis or evidence in an attempt to prevent them from calculating ballots sent to a list of allegedly “likely” ineligible voters and threatened election officials with criminal prosecution. Similar claims of lists from the Trump Administration supposedly identifying ineligible voters have proven overstated or false in the past, and they have included many eligible American voters. Both Padilla and Morelle’s committees have jurisdiction over federal elections in the Senate and House, respectively. “The Department must serve the interests of Americans, not operate at the personal and political direction of the president or to advance the partisan interests of a political party,” the lawmakers wrote. The DOJ itself has admitted that alleged noncitizen lists fabricated by the Trump Administration are unreliable. And while the DOJ’s allegations are entirely speculative, they create unnecessary burdens on California in the middle of an ongoing election that would force California officials to violate federal law. The DOJ’s intent is clear – undermine public confidence in the outcome of California’s elections to further President Trump’s baseless feud with a state that has rejected him three times. “This is the second time in less than four months that the Department has responded to the President’s public demands to interfere in an ongoing election in California, and it is a blatant misuse of the Department’s resources and abuse of the Department’s authority… The Department’s attempt to disenfranchise thousands of American voters en masse , based on no evidence of any individual’s ineligibility, is a clear violation of Californians’ federal constitutional right to vote. The right to vote, of course, is also enshrined in the Constitution of California,” the lawmakers continued. As Ranking Member of the Senate Rules Committee and California’s former Secretary of State and chief election officer, Padilla has fought relentlessly to protect our elections and strengthen voting rights. Last week, Padilla demanded that DOJ commit to not seize ballots or voting equipment during the midterm elections. Last month, Padilla introduced the Freedom from Intimidation in Elections Act , legislation to protect voters and election workers from intimidation and threats of violence at polling places. Padilla also led the congressional response to the bombshell whistleblower report that DHS agents violated state laws as part of the “Unlawful Voter Initiative” and called for an immediate investigation into the agency’s misconduct, which has likely led to the creation of dubious lists of supposedly ineligible voters. He also urged California’s Attorney General to investigate the effects these actions could have on Californians. Also last month, Padilla convened some of the country’s top labor leaders to discuss how to strengthen our democracy and mobilize against election interference. In August, he led 27 of his Senate colleagues in demanding the Trump Administration stop its illegal voter roll purges before Election Day. Padilla also joined Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) in launching the first-ever Senate Election Observer Program to protect the 2026 midterms and maintain election integrity nationwide and serves as part of the Senate Democrats’ Election Protection Task Force. This week, Padilla announced that more than 100 Senate Democratic staff have been recruited and trained as official congressional election observers to be deployed to polling sites across nine states. In June, Padilla joined his colleagues in introducing the Protect Our Polls Act to protect the integrity of American elections from federal interference by armed military or federal law enforcement. Full letter is available here or below : R. Trent McCotter Acting Deputy Attorney General United States Department of Justice 950 Pennsylvania Avenue, NW Washington, D.C. 20530 Dear Acting Deputy Attorney General McCotter: Your October 13, 2026, letters to California Secretary of State Dr. Shirley Weber (the “Letters”) and Dean Logan, Los Angeles County Registrar-Record/County Clerk, the Department of Justice’s (the “Department”) related October 15, 2026, complaint (the “Complaint”), and its October 16, 2026, letter to the Los Angeles County Counsel’s Office raise serious and unprecedented questions about political weaponization at the Department during an ongoing federal election. The Department’s lawsuit and subsequent threat to use federal criminal law to interfere with the mailing and counting of ballots in California rests the on highly suspect legal and intellectual bases and raises questions about the standards of professional responsibility to which the Department should hold its attorneys. The Department must serve the interests of Americans, not operate at the personal and political direction of the president or to advance the partisan interests of a political party. In this instance, it appears that the Department has betrayed its historical duty “to enforce the laws of the United States . . . in a neutral and impartial manner.” As such, we require information from you related to the Department’s decision-making in this matter. The Complaint’s claim “that California will count vote-by-mail ballots of likely noncitizen voters” bears no basis in fact—the Department makes no effort to present any evidence that any individuals included on the Trump Administration’s list of alleged noncitizens are ineligible to vote. Nor does the Department explain with any specificity why it doubts that California will fail to manage its voter rolls properly. Indeed, similar claims from the Trump Administration have proven dismally false in the past. For example, the Department of Homeland Security (“DHS”) made an outlandish and unsubstantiated claim that it had discovered 16,000 noncitizens on Nevada voter rolls—a claim that Nevada officials later determined was flatly incorrect; every person identified by DHS was a lawful United States citizen. In fact, the Department itself has admitted that alleged noncitizenship lists manufactured by the Trump Administration are unreliable. But while the allegations underlying the Letters and the Complaint are entirely conjectural, the relief demanded would impose real and onerous burdens on California in the midst of an ongoing election. And the Department’s design here is clear—undermining public confidence in the outcome of California elections to further President Trump’s longstanding but baseless vendetta against a state that has, on three occasions, voted for the Democratic presidential nominee. This is the second time in less than four months that the Department has responded to the President’s public demands to interfere in an ongoing election in California, and it is a blatant misuse of the Department’s resources and abuse of the Department’s authority. Glaring partisan motivation is not the only fatal flaw in the Department’s machinations. The Complaint plainly demands that California violate state and federal law. The Department’s attempt to disenfranchise thousands of American voters en masse, based on no evidence of any individual’s ineligibility, is a clear violation of Californians’ federal constitutional right to vote. The right to vote, of course, is also enshrined in the Constitution of California. In addition, the Department’s own guidance for compliance with the National Voter Registration Act (“NVRA”) states: “list maintenance activities that may violate the NVRA include comparing voter files to outdated or inaccurate records or databases, taking action that erroneously affects a particular class of voters (such as newly naturalized citizens).” While you falsely accuse California and Los Angeles County officials of criminal violations, the Department’s demands here would violate federal statute: “No person acting under color of law shall fail or refuse to permit any person to vote who is entitled to vote . . . or willfully fail or refuse to tabulate, count, and report such person’s vote.” The Complaint’s baffling claim that California “knows that noncitizens might be registered to vote, and it knows the names of such individuals,” but that the state “still intends to count their vote without verifying the voter’s citizenship,” is, simply, fiction. Despite the Department’s attacks regarding “unverified statements of citizenship necessary to registering,” the truth is that voters in California make an attestation of citizenship under penalty of perjury to register to vote— similar to the vast majority of states and as set forth in federal law. The Department is apparently seeking to create the disastrous and foreseeable outcome that tens of thousands of Americans—people who have already received and potentially cast ballots—could see their votes cast aside based on innuendo and defective data. The Department’s unprecedented demand that California arbitrarily segregate ballots and ignore the state’s legal responsibility to process and tabulate the ballots cast by eligible American voters runs afoul of the Constitution and the rule of law. Further, the Department simply has no legal or constitutional authority to make such a demand on California. The Complaint woefully misstates—or simply misunderstands—the theory of federal preemption. The Department’s extreme demand that a federal court “[d]eclare that California’s actions here . . . are preempted and thus violate the Supremacy Clause,” would effectively abrogate the states’ clear and specific constitutional duty to regulate the time, place, and manner of elections in our Republic. The claims in the Letters and Complaint lack any basis in fact and the Department lacks any basis in legal authority. Finally, the recent behavior of the Department in this and other matters raise serious concerns about the professional integrity and ethical responsibility expected of attorneys by the Department’s leadership. Federal law requires that attorneys at the Department comply with the professional responsibility rules of the states in which they practice. First, the Department of Justice Manual includes an election noninterference policy which states that the Department: “should generally avoid interfering or appearing to interfere with election administration, tabulation, validation, or certification.” Perhaps Americans should not be surprised that the Department is failing to adhere to its own standards when one of the key Department officials involved in threatening California election officials has reportedly stated “f[**]k the Justice Manual” in the context of another politically-motivated attempted criminal prosecution. In addition, the Rules of Professional Conduct of the State Bar of California, for example, make clear that it is professional misconduct for a lawyer to “engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or reckless or intentional misrepresentation,” or “engage in conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice.” The District of Columbia Bar holds its attorneys to almost identical standards. And as a recent opinion of the American Bar Association makes clear: all lawyers, including government lawyers, have a responsibility to abide by the professional conduct rules applicable to their own conduct . . . and, if the direction provided by the supervisor is “a reasonable resolution of an arguable question of professional duty,” the subordinate may defer to it even if the subordinate would decide the issue differently. However, unless the superior’s direction meets that standard, following orders is no excuse and the subordinate lawyer is responsible for the lawyer’s own conduct. In both the Letters and the Complaint, the Department’s stated motivations are spurious; they poorly conceal an unmistakable—and unethical—improper partisan motivation that comes through even more clearly in Department officials’ social media posts. Both the October 13 letter and the Complaint misrepresent the law and overstate the Department’s authority. And, in both the Letters and the Complaint, the Department attempts to subvert a free and fair American election. Any Department staff engaged in this effort should be wary as lapses in an attorney’s professional responsibilities have far-reaching, and expensive, repercussions. In order to safeguard American elections, Congress must determine whether additional legislation is necessary to address the brazen misuse of the Department’s law enforcement powers for partisan purposes—in California or in any other state or jurisdiction in which the Department is considering, or may consider in the future, similar illegal action. Accordingly, in exercise of Congress’s oversight and legislative authority, we request that you provide the following information and materials no later than 5:00 p.m. on November 2, 2026: Did the White House direct any aspects of the decision-making related to the Letters or the Complaint, or was the White House aware of or involved in any other way in developing and implementing the steps leading to and including the lawsuit against California? How, and on what basis, did DHS or the Department identify the names provided to California? Who was involved in the process by which these names were identified? Did private parties provide any of the data that DHS or the Department delivered to California? If so, how much? Why did the Department wait until now, weeks before the election, to first threaten California through the Letters and file the Complaint if, as the Department alleges, this data was assembled months ago? Who was involved in the decision to send the October 13, 2026, letter to California and subsequently to file the Complaint? For purposes of robust congressional oversight, please identify the specific senior advisory personnel who were responsible, including any who may have relevant information about the process. Please also specifically identify every Department, other administration agency, or private party lawyer, who worked on the October 13, 2026, letter, the October 16, 2026, letter, or Complaint. Did the Department consult private parties, or did such parties advise, upon the “legal theory” advanced in the Complaint against California? What, precisely, does the Department mean when it refers to “thousands of likely noncitizens registered to vote in California”? What threshold of “likelihood” did the DHS or the Department establish (especially considering the previous, and extensively erroneous, citizenship identification lists the Trump Administration has produced for other states)? Please provide the complete matching methodology and criteria used to build the supposed list of noncitizens registered in the state of California. Identify every official who validated the list before it was given to a local election office. Did any DHS personnel misrepresent themselves as California voters when attempting to access California voter data as part of the process to identify these names? Federal law bars systematic voter purges within 90 days of a federal election. California mailed ballots on October 5, and the Department filed its complaint 19 days before Election Day. Did the Department’s lawyers produce any analysis of whether its request violates federal law? Please either produce said analysis or confirm none was conducted. Did Department leadership or any individual involved in drafting the Letters or the Complaint consult the Department’s Office of Professional Responsibility or Department ethics counsel regarding the clear ethical and policy questions presented by the Department’s unprecedented constitutional claim to threaten, and then file suit against, a state within weeks of the November elections? If so, what advice was received? If no consultation took place, explain why. Did DHS and the Department follow established agency cybersecurity practices in the creation, and transmittal, of the thumb drive delivered to Los Angeles Couty? If so, please delineate the precise guidelines DHS and the Department followed. If not, please explain why the Trump Administration chose to jeopardize both the private personal information of thousands of American citizens and the election infrastructure of Los Angeles County. Who approved this method of delivery of sensitive voter data? As Ranking Member of the Committee on House Administration and a member of the House Appropriations subcommittee with oversight of the Department, and Ranking Member of the Senate Committee on Rules and Administration, who represents the State of California, we look forward to your prompt transmittal of the above requested information. Thank you for your attention to this matter. Sincerely, Alex Padilla — United States Senator, Ranking Member, Committee on Rules and Administration Joseph D. Morelle — Member of Congress, Ranking Member, Committee on House Administration ###

WASHINGTON, D.C. — U.S. Senators Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), Mazie Hirono (D-Hawaii), Tammy Baldwin (D-Wis.), Dick Durbin (D-Ill.), and Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.), along with U.S. Representatives Grace Meng (D-N.Y.-06), Adriano Espaillat (D-N.Y.-13), and Yvette Clarke (D-N.Y.-09), pressed U.S. Department of Education (ED) Secretary Linda McMahon on the Administration’s illegal decision to redirect funding from Minority-Serving Institutions (MSIs) to other institutions. In their letter to Secretary McMahon, the lawmakers emphasized that, while increasing funding for those institutions is important, the additional investments cannot come at the expense of MSIs that serve millions of students nationwide. The lawmakers also reiterated the illegal nature of the decision to redirect funding that was statutorily authorized in specific amounts for specific purposes. “This administration unnecessarily reallocated half of these funds in order to put out a press release leading up to midterm elections touting how much funding it was providing to HBCUs and Tribal Colleges—while robbing MSIs of investments Congress has provided them. It is offensive that the Trump administration is pitting these institutions of higher education and the students they serve against each other, and going to extra lengths to do so,” wrote the lawmakers . There are currently more than 800 federally recognized MSIs which include Hispanic-Serving Institutions (HSIs), Asian American and Native American Pacific Islander-Serving Institutions (AANAPISIs), Alaska Native and Native Hawaiian-Serving Institutions (ANNHSIs), Native American-Serving Non-Tribal Institutions (NASNTIs), and Predominantly Black Institutions (PBIs). These MSIs serve more than five million students collectively and have been receiving Congressionally directed federal support for more than 30 years. In December 2019, the bipartisan Fostering Undergraduate Talent by Unlocking Resources for Education Act (FUTURE Act) was signed into law, permanently authorizing $255 million in mandatory funding for Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs), Tribally Controlled Colleges and Universities (TCCUs), and MSIs. “The law is clear. Congress mandated that funds, with specific statutorily prescribed amounts, be provided for each grant program with specific statutorily defined purposes in each fiscal year,” continued the lawmakers . The lawmakers outlined how the mandatory funding from the FUTURE Act leaves no room for the Trump Administration to redirect funding from MSIs to any other programs or purpose. “To be clear, mandatory funding for [these institutions]—as provided by the FUTURE Act—cannot be reallocated for other purposes or programs without explicit authorization from Congress. ED does not have the unilateral authority to reallocate these funds,” wrote the lawmakers. The lawmakers reiterated the importance of supporting all institutions supporting minority students—including HBCUs and TCCUs. “ED must immediately remedy these illegal actions and restore the funds that were illegally taken away from HSIs, AANAPISIs, ANNHSIs, NASNTIs, and PBIs,” the lawmakers concluded. “Increases in funding for HBCUs and TCCUs should not come at the expense of other critical institutions of higher education.” In addition to Padilla, Hirono, Sanders, Murray, Baldwin, Durbin, and Luján, the letter was cosigned by Senators Chris Coons (D-Del.), Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.), Jack Reed (D-R.I.), Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), Tim Kaine (D-Va.), Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.), Adam Schiff (D-Calif.), Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii), Ed Markey (D-Mass.), Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), Cory Booker (D-N.J.), Andy Kim (D-N.J.), Jacky Rosen (D-Nev.), Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.), Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.), Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.), Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Mark Warner (D-Va.), Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.), and Michael Bennet (D-Colo.). In addition to Representatives Meng, Espaillat, and Clarke, the letter was also cosigned by Representatives Eleanor Holmes Norton (D-D.C.-AL), Mark Takano (D-Calif.-39), Danny Davis (D-Ill.-07), Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-Ill.-08), Judy Chu (D-Calif.-28), Jesus “Chuy” Garcia (D-Ill.-07), Dina Titus (D-Nev.-01), Paul Tonko (D-N.Y.-20), Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.-01), Jill Tokuda (D-Hawaii-02), Robin Kelly (D-Ill.-02), Jimmy Gomez (D-Calif.-34), Mark DeSaulnier (D-Calif.-10), Emily Randall (D-Wash.-06), Jasmine Crockett (D-Texas-30), Joaquin Castro (D-Texas-30), Ed Case (D-Hawaii-01), J. Correa (D-Calif.-46), Susan Bonamici (D-Ore.-01), Sylvia Garcia (D-Texas-29), Robert Menendez (D-N.J.-08), Ted Lieu (D-Calif.-36), Mike Thompson (D-Calif.-04), Derek Tran (D-Calif.-45), Lateefah Simon (D-Calif.-12), George Whitesides (D-Calif.-27), Salud Carbajal (D-Calif.-24), Greg Stanton (D-Ariz.-04), Linda Sánchez (D-Calif.-38), Chellie Pingree (D-Maine-01), Darren Soto (D-Fla.-09), Juan Vargas (D-Calif.-52), Teresa Leger Fernández (D-N.M.-03), Adelita Grijalva (D-Ariz.-07), Jennifer McClellan (D-Va.-04), Kevin Mullin (D-Calif.-15), and Robert Garcia (D-Calif.-42). As chair of the Senate HSI Caucus, Padilla has led the fight opposing the Trump Administration’s attacks on MSIs. In February, Padilla demanded the Department of Education immediately reverse its decision to deem MSIs unconstitutional and cut off federal funding. Last year, Padilla also led multiple letters opposing the Department of Education’s decision to rescind $350 million in funding from MSIs, including a letter with members from the California delegation about the impact directly on California. Full text of the letter is available here and below: Dear Secretary McMahon: Your recent decision to reallocate mandatory funding for Minority-Serving Institutions (MSIs) in Fiscal Year 2025 and Fiscal Year 2026 is an illegal violation of Congress’ spending authority under the Constitution. No court has found these programs that Congress has funded to be unconstitutional, and the administration’s mere belief that they are does not give it the necessary authority to spend those funds for any other purpose or program. Many of us previously sent you a letter urging you to allocate Title III and Title V discretionary and mandatory funds as Congress directed to the more than 800 federally-recognized MSIs, which include Hispanic-Serving Institutions (HSIs), Asian American and Native American Pacific Islander-Serving Institutions (AANAPISIs), Alaska Native and Native Hawaiian-Serving Institutions (ANNHSIs), Native American-Serving Non-Tribal Institutions (NASNTIs), and Predominantly Black Institutions (PBIs). Combined, these institutions enroll more than 5 million students in rural and urban communities in states across the country. The Higher Education Act created the statutory framework for grants to these institutions, and has been in place for more than 30 years. In December 2019, Congress passed and President Trump signed into law the bipartisan Fostering Undergraduate Talent by Unlocking Resources for Education Act (FUTURE Act), permanently authorizing $255 million in grant funds for MSIs, Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs), and Tribally Controlled Colleges and Universities (TCCUs). The funds are allocated across seven grant programs, each with a designated funding amount beginning in Fiscal Year 2020 and continuing thereafter. This authorization was an extension of prior mandatory appropriations that began in Fiscal Year 2008 and then expired. Reallocation of Funds Designated for HSIs, AANAPISIs, ANNHSIs, and NASNTIs On September 22, 2026, the U.S. Department of Education (ED) announced it would reallocate FY25 and FY26 mandatory funds Congress had specifically allocated for MSIs to HBCUs and TCCUs. In the news release announcing this illegal action, ED announced a “significant, one-time investment of more than $174 million in additional funding to strengthen” HBCUs, and “a one-time award of more than $61 million in additional funding” for TCCUs. While we strongly support additional funding for HBCUs and TCCUs, increasing funding for some institutions should not come at the expense of others. Furthermore, as previously stated, ED has no authority to redirect mandatory funding for MSIs—in this case, for HSIs, AANAPISIs, ANNHSIs, and NASNTIs—for other purposes or programs. In fact, the entire basis for invalidating and redistributing these funds seems to be a U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) Office of Legal Counsel (OLC) opinion from December 2, 2025, which wrongly determined that both discretionary and mandatory grants for HSIs, AANAPISIs, ANNHSIs, and NASNTIs, and discretionary grants for PBIs, were unconstitutional—without any judicial decision squarely dictating such a conclusion, and lacking any statutory authority to spend mandatory funds for anything other than their required purposes. Shortly thereafter, ED stated that it was evaluating the full impact of the OLC opinion on the programs. ED then took several actions which made clear that it would not fund the programs, including by not allowing institutions to reapply for eligibility for the programs, and not including them in the eligibility matrix for Title III and Title V funds. Reallocation of Funds Designated for PBIs Even by its own baseless standards, the administration determined in the December 2025 OLC memo that the race-based provisions of this program could be severed and stated that ED could continue to provide these competitive grants for the authorized uses in this program, regardless of whether the grant recipient is a PBI. However, rather than adhering to the statute authorizing this grant program—or even OLC’s own wrongful guidance—ED allocated these funds to grantees under a different program with a separate purpose. Unnecessarily Accelerating Obligation of FY26 Mandatory Funds On top of all of this, the Trump administration took the completely unnecessary step of obligating FY26 mandatory funding for these programs a full year before it has historically been done, and a full year before the funds expire. These funds are available for two years—funds becoming available in FY26 are available for obligation through FY27. If ED only continued to award funds on the schedule it has historically, FY26 funds would be awarded this time next year. The administration has claimed it reallocated these funds so they did not lapse and go to waste. While the Trump administration is perfectly willing to let appropriated funds lapse in other cases, including most recently with international education and migrant and seasonal farmworker education programs, half of the MSI funds it reallocated were not going to lapse this year. Even if one were to take the administration’s misguided legal view of these programs at face value, for half of these funds the choice was not between reallocating funding or having the funds lapse. The administration has said repeatedly it wants to work with Congress on solutions to address the legal status of these programs. While we fundamentally disagree with the administration’s view, the administration could have simply continued to administer these funds on the timeline it always has—which means obligating the FY26 funds next September—and waited to see if Congress enacted a solution or a court ruled on the constitutionality of these programs over the course of the next year. In fact, Congress did enact a temporary and albeit imperfect fix in the FY26 Consolidated Appropriations Act when faced with the fact that the Trump administration would otherwise let discretionary funding for MSIs lapse. This administration unnecessarily reallocated half of these funds in order to put out a press release leading up to midterm elections touting how much funding it was providing to HBCUs and Tribal Colleges—while robbing MSIs of investments Congress has provided them. It is offensive that the Trump administration is pitting these institutions of higher education and the students they serve against each other, and going to extra lengths to do so. If President Trump and this administration were serious about investing in all of these institutions—as each of us is—the president would push for more funds for them instead of seeking to slash education programs while supersizing the Pentagon’s budget. The law is clear. Congress mandated that funds, with specific statutorily prescribed amounts, be provided for each grant program with specific statutorily defined purposes in each fiscal year. To be clear, mandatory funding for HBCUs, TCCUs, HSIs, AANAPISIs, ANNHSIs, NASNTIs, and PBIs—as provided by the FUTURE Act—cannot be reallocated for other purposes or programs without explicit authorization from Congress. ED does not have the unilateral authority to reallocate these funds. The Executive Branch’s improper use of mandatory funds plainly violates Article I of the Constitution, which delegates the spending power to Congress. By failing to follow the law and fund programs as Congress directed, and to instead allocate funds for other unauthorized purposes, the Executive Branch has clearly exceeded its Constitutional authority. ED must immediately remedy these illegal actions and restore the funds that were illegally taken away from HSIs, AANAPISIs, ANNHSIs, NASNTIs, and PBIs. Increases in funding for HBCUs and TCCUs should not come at the expense of other critical institutions of higher education. We would welcome the opportunity to work on a bipartisan basis with the administration to increase investments in MSIs, HBCUs, and TCCUs. Thank you for your attention to this urgent matter. We look forward to your response. Sincerely, ###

Following new DOJ demand to block certain ballots in California, Senators urge DOJ to follow the law and reaffirm its longstanding election non-interference policy ahead of 2026 midterm elections, warning that “DOJ action that could spoil an election would be one of the most serious constitutional violations imaginable.” WASHINGTON, D.C. — U.S. Senator Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), Ranking Member of the Senate Committee on Rules and Administration with jurisdiction over federal elections, Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-Ill.), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, and U.S. Senator Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), Ranking Member of the Senate Subcommittee on Federal Courts, Oversight, Agency Action and Federal Rights, demanded that Attorney General Todd Blanche confirm that the Department of Justice (DOJ) will not seize ballots, voting machines, or other election materials in connection with the 2026 midterm elections. Padilla recently secured a commitment under oath from Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) Director Kash Patel that the FBI would not interfere in this year’s midterms, specifically that it would not seize ballots or voting equipment before an election is certified. The letter was sent the same day that the DOJ sued California to block the state from counting alleged noncitizen mail-in ballots less than three weeks before the midterm elections. In the letter to Blanche, the Senators pressed him to reaffirm DOJ’s longstanding policy of election non-interference and commit that it will not pursue any effort to seize ballots or other election materials until all elections have concluded and election results have been certified, given DOJ leadership’s lack of response to earlier inquiries and troubling actions and statements by DOJ when it comes to elections. The letter follows the unprecedented demand by DOJ to the California Secretary of State and Los Angeles County to withhold and segregate ballots from individuals on a list on a USB thumb drive provided by DOJ less than three weeks before Election Day. “Mail and absentee ballots have already been sent out to millions of voters, and early voting has begun in several states,” wrote the Senators . “However, the Department has failed to affirm its election non-interference policy against a backdrop of the recent weakening of DOJ policies, upheaval in the agency’s workforce, DOJ’s seizure of 2020 election materials in Georgia and Arizona, personal calls by President Trump directly to DOJ attorneys to influence election-related investigations in California and elsewhere, as well as unprecedented partisan political activity by DOJ leadership. A clear and immediate response from the Department is necessary.” The Senators highlighted several reasons to be concerned about the Trump Administration’s election interference efforts, including DOJ’s quiet removal of the most recent version of the Federal Prosecution of Election Offenses manual from its website without explanation. They further outlined DOJ’s lack of explanation when pressed for answers and reiterated the unlawfulness of any DOJ effort to interfere in the 2026 midterm elections. “Removing ballots from the officials legally charged with maintaining their custody could prevent election officials from satisfying statutory deadlines, interfere with recount or contest procedures, and even prevent lawful votes from being counted or an election from being certified,” continued the Senators . “Any DOJ action that could spoil an election would be one of the most serious constitutional violations imaginable.” The Senators reiterated the importance of the DOJ reaffirming its election non-interference policy with less than 20 days until Election Day. “The 2026 midterm elections have begun. We urge you to immediately reaffirm that the Department will forgo any actions that would interfere with the lawful administration of the 2026 elections, including the seizure of ballots, election materials, or election equipment prior to the certification of the 2026 midterm elections,” the Senators concluded . Padilla also led the congressional response to the bombshell whistleblower report that DHS agents violated state laws as part of the “Unlawful Voter Initiative” and called for an immediate investigation into the agency’s misconduct. Also last month, Padilla convened some of the country’s top labor leaders to discuss how to strengthen our democracy and mobilize against election interference. In August, he led 27 of his Senate colleagues in demanding the Trump Administration stop its illegal voter roll purges before Election Day. Padilla also joined Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) in launching the first-ever Senate Election Observer Program to protect the 2026 midterms and maintain election integrity nationwide and serves as part of the Senate Democrats’ Election Protection Task Force. This week, Padilla announced that more than 100 Senate Democratic staff have been recruited and trained as official congressional election observers to be deployed to polling sites across nine states. In June, Padilla joined his colleagues in introducing the Protect Our Polls Act to protect the integrity of American elections from federal interference by armed military or federal law enforcement. Full letter is available here or below: Dear Attorney General Blanche: As Election Day draws nearer, we urge the Department of Justice (DOJ or Department) to reaffirm its longstanding election non-interference policy and rule out any attempt to seize ballots or any other election materials or equipment before voting, counting, and/or certification are complete. This confirmation is necessary because Department leaders have been sending conflicting public signals. Make no doubt, the 2026 midterm elections are well underway. Mail and absentee ballots have already been sent out to millions of voters, and early voting has begun in several states. However, the Department has failed to affirm its election non-interference policy against a backdrop of the recent weakening of DOJ policies. A clear and immediate response from the Department is necessary. Recent Statements Regarding the Department’s Election Non-Interference Policy In response to a question during a September 15 public hearing before the Senate Judiciary Committee, Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) Director Kash Patel did confirm under oath that the FBI would comply with the Department’s Justice Manual and not seize ballots, voting machines, or other election-related material prior to certification of an election, matching the commitment by General Dan Caine, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff that the U.S. Armed Forces would not interfere with the upcoming election. However, the FBI Director reports to the Attorney General, so his commitment is contingent on your own. On September 1, Senator Slotkin wrote to you and Director Patel seeking answers to a number of questions, including whether DOJ or the FBI would send armed federal agents to the polls or unlawfully seize election materials of any kind during an active election. To date, neither you nor Director Patel have responded to those letters. Meanwhile, General Caine did respond to a similar letter and reaffirmed the “non-partisan” U.S. Armed Forces’ “steadfast commitment to constitutional principles” and confirmed that the military had “no plans to send Federal military personnel or Federalized members of the National Guard to polling places during the 2026 elections” and “[n]o plans to use such personnel to seize ballots, voting machines, or other election-related material.” On June 8, 2026, Senators Padilla, Durbin, Whitehouse, and 21 Senators wrote to you regarding the Department’s unexplained removal from its website of the most recent version of the Federal Prosecution of Election Offenses manual (Election Crimes Manual) that has been in place for decades to prevent the Department from interfering or appearing to interfere in elections. The Department’s August 13 response states that the manual “needs revising and updating” but provided no further explanation, and an updated version has yet to be made available to the public. DOJ Election Interference is Illegal The law is clear: neither the Department nor any other federal agency has the authority to disrupt the administration of an election, including by seizing ballots or other election materials in a manner that prevents state and local officials from carrying out their lawful duties. The U.S. Constitution gives primary authority over elections to the states and Congress, not the Executive Branch, and federal law reinforces these constitutional provisions. The Civil Rights Act of 1960 requires election officers to “retain and preserve” covered election records for 22 months following a federal election. If a federal agency seeks access to election materials, the law requires an appropriate written demand, after which covered records are to be made available for federal “inspection, reproduction, and copying” at the principal office of their custodian. Even this authority is limited, as shown by DOJ’s failure to compel Republican and Democratic-led states alike to hand over unredacted voter data for the Trump Administration to create a national voter file and pressure states to purge voters under the guise of list maintenance. Federal law enforcement must also respect detailed state laws governing custody of ballots and voting equipment. Maintaining an unbroken chain of custody ensures that the ballots ultimately counted are the ballots American voters actually cast. Removing ballots from the officials legally charged with maintaining their custody could prevent election officials from satisfying statutory deadlines, interfere with recount or contest procedures, and even prevent lawful votes from being counted or an election from being certified. Any DOJ action that could spoil an election would be one of the most serious constitutional violations imaginable. The Justice Manual and the Election Crimes Manual The same commitment made by General Caine and Director Patel should represent the position of the Trump Administration. The Department’s Justice Manual unequivocally recognizes the constitutional requirement that “the States—not the federal government—are responsible for administering elections.” While DOJ’s “non-interference policy” was incorporated into the Justice Manual in 2022, it has been in effect through the DOJ Election Crimes Branch for decades. This enduring bipartisan policy reflects the fundamental principle that DOJ and other law enforcement personnel should not interfere with the will of the American people. The Justice Manual’s “non-interference policy” states that DOJ “should generally avoid interfering or appearing to interfere with election administration, tabulation, validation, or certification.” It further provides that DOJ “should not engage in overt criminal investigative measures in matters involving alleged ballot fraud until the election in question has been concluded, its results certified, and all recounts and election contests concluded.” However, the removal of the Election Crimes Manual from the DOJ website remains of special concern because it contains even more explicit instructions against actions that “may deprive state election and judicial authorities of critical materials needed to resolve election disputes, conduct recounts, and certify ultimate winners.” In addition to avoiding seizures, the Election Crimes Manual further confirms the DOJ policy not to conduct overt investigations until after the outcome of the election has been certified. Adding to the concern, pending revisions to the Justice Manual are creating new uncertainty. The requirement that prosecutors and agents consult with the Public Integrity Section before opening an election-crime matter or undertaking any potentially overt investigative steps—including issuing grand jury subpoenas and executing search warrants—has been “suspended while revisions are ongoing.” Given that it is too late for revisions ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, DOJ should restore this part of its election policy immediately. Failure to maintain a strong, explicit election non-interference policy exposes DOJ prosecutors to political pressure to interfere in elections at the request of the President or other Administration leaders, political parties, candidates, and other influences. The Department Must Reaffirm Its Election Non-Interference Policy The 2026 midterm elections have begun. We urge you to immediately reaffirm that the Department will forgo any actions that would interfere with the lawful administration of the 2026 elections, including the seizure of ballots, election materials, or election equipment prior to the certification of the 2026 midterm elections. In addition to this immediate public commitment, we request that you provide written responses to the following questions by October 29, 2026: 1) Will you commit that DOJ, the FBI, the U.S. Marshals Service, and other Department components will not attempt to seize or otherwise remove ballots, voting equipment, or other election materials from the lawful custody of state or local election officials while those materials are necessary for voting, counting, canvassing, recounting, auditing, election contests, or certification? a) Will you commit not to approve or otherwise facilitate any attempts by any other federal law enforcement agency, including components of the Department of Homeland Security, to take similar actions? 2) Does DOJ continue to adhere to the guidance contained in the eighth edition of the Election Crimes Manual that election-related documents generally should not be removed from local election administrators before certification and expiration of the applicable election-contest period, and that election officials should not be deprived of documents necessary to tally or recount ballots or certify election results? a) What provisions of the Election Crimes Manual require “revising and updating” as stated in the Department’s previous response letter? Does the Election Crimes Manual remain the policy of the Department, and, if not, has the Department rescinded, superseded, amended, or otherwise withdrawn the eighth edition? b) If revisions are underway, provide the current draft, identify the officials responsible for those revisions, and state when the revised guidance will be made public. 3) Does DOJ continue to adhere fully to Justice Manual §§ 9-85.300 and 9-85.500, including the prohibition that “[f]ederal prosecutors and agents may never select the timing of any action, including investigative steps, criminal charges, or statements, for the purpose of affecting any election, or for the purpose of giving an advantage or disadvantage to any candidate or political party”? 4) Given that the Justice Manual currently states that the election-crimes consultation requirement in § 9-85.210 is suspended while revisions are underway, what review and approval procedures currently govern applications for search warrants, subpoenas, or other overt investigative measures involving ballots, voting equipment, election officials, or other election materials during an active election? a) When will the revisions of the manual be complete and available to the public? 5) Has the Department, the FBI, any United States Attorney’s Office, or any other Department component developed, discussed, requested, sought judicial authorization for, or approved any plan to seize ballots, voting machines, tabulation equipment, or other election materials relating to the 2026 federal elections before completion of the applicable counting, recounting, canvassing, contest, and certification processes? a) If so, provide all applicable policies, legal analyses, directives, memoranda, and approval procedures concerning such actions. Thank you for your prompt response. ###

Ranking Members also press DOJ and FBI to provide information related to the agencies’ coordination with DHS, the U.S. Intelligence Community, and the White House in these efforts to undermine our election security WASHINGTON, D.C. — Today, U.S. Senator Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), Ranking Member of the Senate Rules and Administration Committee, Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-Ill.), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, and Senators Mark Warner, Vice Chair of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, and Gary Peters, Ranking Member of the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, demanded answers regarding the alarming series of actions the Trump Administration has undertaken to undermine state and local election administration. In a letter to Attorney General Todd Blanche and Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) Director Kash Patel, the Senators raised concerns about the extent of the Department of Justice’s (DOJ) and FBI’s coordination with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), the U.S. Intelligence Community, and the White House in efforts to interfere with the midterm elections. “Under your leadership, DOJ and the FBI have sought to upend our federalist system by seizing ballots and election materials, seeking the personal information of election workers and volunteers, showing up at the homes of election officials for questioning, threatening election officials with prosecution, attempting to compel states to provide the federal government with unredacted voter rolls, and raiding the offices of a voting rights nonprofit—often at the apparent behest of President Trump and White House officials, including Stephen Miller,” wrote the Senators . “Director Patel has reportedly urged the FBI to persist in these fishing expeditions by exhorting agents to ‘look harder’ because ‘this is a push from 47,’ and senior DOJ officials have threatened to fire or override prosecutors who choose not to pursue election fraud cases that FBI or DHS agents bring them, in contravention of longstanding DOJ rules for prosecutors.” The Senators outlined the timeline of the Trump Administration’s attempted efforts to undermine elections. The weaponization of DOJ and the FBI as part of this effort became clear last year, when the head of the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division (CRT) began filing lawsuits against multiple states to demand they produce unredacted copies of their voter registration lists. CRT sued Fulton County, Georgia last December, seeking records related to the 2020 election. Following this lawsuit, the FBI executed a search warrant at the Fulton County election office in Union City, Georgia. Additionally, then-Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard inexplicably attended this raid—and escalated this breach of protocol the following day, when she met with FBI agents who had conducted the raid and called President Trump to address the agents. “These efforts have occurred as U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) has taken unprecedented steps to investigate unfounded claims of widespread voter fraud and as the then-Director of National Intelligence took extraordinary steps to insert herself into an already-troubling FBI raid of a local election facility,” continued the Senators . “Taken together, these actions constitute a disturbing, whole-of-government campaign that has weaponized federal law enforcement to relitigate the 2020 election that President Trump lost, attempting to undermine the constitutional election administration powers of states ahead of the 2026 midterm elections and seeking to sow confusion and fear among voters and state and local election officials.” The Senators also raised concerns about Patel refusing to rule out sending FBI agents to polling locations on Election Day—an illegal tactic that would inevitably intimidate voters. “The concern over this Administration engaging in intimidation tactics related to the election is not unwarranted,” wrote the Senators . “Just one month before election day, President Trump continues to float the idea that he has legal authority to declare a national emergency or invoke the Insurrection Act around the midterms. Moreover, DOJ has already sought to intimidate election officials across the country.” Just this week, the DOJ attempted to escalate these efforts, laying the groundwork to potentially challenge ballots ahead of Election Day with a letter to California election officials, which demanded that they verify the citizenship of individuals listed in a DOJ-provided thumb drive within 48 hours and threatened legal action if they do not follow the Department’s instructions on handling the ballots of these individuals. “Furthermore, it is impossible to ignore the brazen partisan intentions behind these actions—not just due to President Trump’s repeated, baseless accusations that Democrats must cheat to win elections, but in light of the unethical political actions you have each taken in recent weeks, including your appearances at an August campaign rally in New York, and Attorney General Blanche’s appearance at the Republican Party’s midterm convention in Texasand a campaign event in North Carolina for Republican Senate nominee Michael Whatley,” the Senators concluded . “It is our constitutional duty to conduct oversight over these unprecedented abuses of power to improperly meddle with state and local election administration in the midterm elections that are already underway. The American people deserve to know why federal resources are being diverted from mission critical work to ensure their safety and instead devoted to this costly and, should it further escalate, potentially criminal crusade.” The Senators also noted that despite this brazen, partisan, and coordinated effort to undermine the constitutional structure of our democracy, the rule of law will prevail—countless patriotic Americans across the country are working tirelessly to combat this chaos and distrust and ensure that every eligible American is able to cast their ballot and that their vote is counted. Americans should have confidence that their voices will be heard in November and that these efforts by the Trump Administration to weaponize federal law enforcement to meddle in the midterm elections will ultimately fail. Padilla has consistently advocated for protection against the Trump Administration’s election interference efforts. Padilla joined Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) in launching the first-ever Senate Election Observer Program to protect the 2026 midterms and maintain election integrity nationwide and serves as part of the Senate Democrats’ Election Protection Task Force.
